paragraphs.text: INTRODUCTION TO THE DIVINE SCRIPTURES (1). There are three kinds of idiom in the Hebrew style: one is found in the sense, another in the wording, and another in the arrangement of words. Beginning of the idioms of sense. The idiom of sense is the practice of describing God's activities, whether they work for good or for ill, in terms of things that belong to us. I mean in terms of limbs, or senses, or movements of the soul, or movements of the body, or passions of the soul, or passions of the body, or dispositions, or common conventions, or ranks, or occupations, or places, or clothing, or customs, or gestures, or the whole living being. 1. How it does this from limbs. From limbs, as in: "His eyelids examine the children of men"; and: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous"; and: "The mouth of the Lord has spoken these things"; and: "The law of your mouth is good to me"; and: "Surely righteousness shall go forth from my mouth"; and: "The face of the Lord is against those who do evil"; and: "Lift up your hands against their arrogance." It usually names the right hand for the better things, because the right hand is more honourable. For example: "The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds"; and: "Let us worship at the place where his feet stood"; and whatever is like these. Of these expressions, some are used for salvation and others for punishment. 2. How it does this from the senses. As in: "The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the children of men"; and: "With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me"; and: "The Lord will hear me"; and: "The Lord smelled a pleasing fragrance"; and: "Send forth your hand"; and: "[?] his bones"; and: "The hand of the Lord that has touched me"; and: "He who touches the mountains, and they smoke"; and: "I will feel out all the iniquity of that land"; and: "Shall I eat the flesh of bulls?" And the Saviour says: "I have food to eat that you do not know"; and: "My food is that I [(1) Introduction to the Holy Scriptures. Photius: "Adrian's Introduction to Scripture was read; the book is useful to beginners."]

do the will of my Father." And the swiftness of [?] (Ps. 23:15; 3:5; 4:4; Gen. 8 [?]), as in: "He mounted upon cherubim and flew." 3. From movements of the soul. As in: "I trampled them in my wrath and crushed them in my anger" (2); and: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger." 4. From movements of the body. As in: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered"; and: "Awake, O Lord my God, in the command that you commanded"; and: "Wait for me until the day of my rising up"; and: "Adam heard God walking." 5. From passions of the soul. As in: "I repented, says God, that I made man"; and: "God tested Abraham"; and: "You have forgotten the law of your God; I too will forget your children."

6. From passions of the body. As in: "Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?"; and: "The Lord awoke like one who sleeps"; and: "He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep"; and similar passages. 7. From dispositions. As in: "Was not Esau Jacob's brother?"; and: "I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated"; and: "The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob"; and: "I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy." 8. From common conventions. As in: "I will betroth you to myself forever"; and: "I will betroth you in judgement and in righteousness"; and: "She is not my wife, and I am not her husband"; and: "And I gave her a bill of divorce"; and: "I became a father to Israel"; and: "Ephraim is my firstborn"; and: "He shall call upon me, 'You are my Father,' and I will make him my firstborn"; and: "Israel is my firstborn son"; and similar passages. 9. From ranks. As in: "The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice"; and: "You who are seated upon the cherubim, shine forth"; and: "You sat upon a throne, judging righteousness." 10. From occupations. As in: "He who roofs with [NOTES. [?] ... of a friend than the unwilling kisses of an enemy [?]. More trustworthy are the wounds of friends than the unwilling kisses of enemies. Eccles. [?]]

waters his upper chambers"; and: "He formed man"; and: "He breathed into his face the breath of life"; and: "He has come up, breathing into your face." This means: "With blasts of breath he scatters your adversaries before your eyes"; that is, so easily and all at once. Pagan writers too took "breathing upon" to mean "scattering." And to Jerusalem: "Behold, on my hand I have painted your walls"; and: "I put a hedge around it, and fenced it, and planted you as a choice vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and dug a winepress in it"; and: "Behold, I will hedge up her way with thorns, and I will rebuild her paths, and she shall not find her way"; and: "I will spread my net over him"; and: "Sinners shall fall into his casting-net"; and whatever is similar. 11. From places. As in: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God"; and: "You ascended on high; you led captivity captive"; and: "He bowed the heavens and came down"; and: "The Lord is near to those who call upon him"; and: "Why, O Lord, do you stand far off?"; and: "Behold, the Lord sits upon a swift cloud"; and: "Behold, the Lord comes forth from his place"; and: "He will tread upon the high places of the

12. From clothing. As in: "The Lord has clothed himself with power and girded himself"; and: "Gird your sword upon your thigh"; and: "Girded with might"; and: "Wrapping himself in light as in a garment"; and: "Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments reddened from Bozrah, this one splendid in his apparel?" 13. From customs. As in: "You turned away your face, and I was troubled"; and: "Why, O Lord, do you cast off my soul? Why do you turn your face away?"; and: "Do not turn aside in anger from your servant"; and: "Do not cast me away from your face"; and: "But I said in my alarm, 'I am cast away from the sight of your eyes.'" These are things that people who are angry and grieved display toward those they are at odds with. 14. From gestures. As in: "Why do you turn away your hand, even your right hand?" This is a metaphor drawn from people who are being entreated and turn their hands behind them. And: "For I will lift up my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand"; and the

15. From the whole living being. From the whole living being taken in its parts: sometimes from the soul, sometimes from the flesh. As in Hosea: "My flesh is from them." From the soul, as in: "My soul hates your new moons and your Sabbaths." These are given as examples, to set out more fully the reasons behind the idioms. Explanation of the divisions listed above. 1 and 2. The fact that nothing escapes God's knowledge Scripture usually calls eyes, eyelids and sight,

both for good, as in: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous," and for ill: "His eyes look upon the nations." 3. His readiness to be appeased it calls ears and hearing, and what reveals his will it calls speech and mouth. And because among us the thoughts of the mind are made known through the mouth and words, it also calls our concurrence with what he wills his food, since among us the satisfying of natural need comes about through the sense of taste. 4. His acceptance of our goodwill toward him it calls smelling. 5. His manifestation in events it calls his face, since among us it is by the face that a person appears, whether for good or for ill. As in: "But the face of the Lord is against those who do

6. The effectiveness of his activity it names hands, since among us the most necessary things are accomplished through the work of the hands, whether for good or for ill. As in: "Send forth your hand from on high"; and: "Lift up your hands against their arrogance to the end." 7. The right hand, however, it seems to use only of favourable things, as being the more honourable part. 8. And his precision in acting, put more intensely, it calls feeling or touching; while his inclination to help those in need it names feet and walking. As in: "And he bowed the heavens and came down"; and: "Adam heard God walking in paradise." 9. It also often keeps the figure consistent throughout. In the psalm, for instance, it depicts God as coming down, then crying out, then sending arrows. It does the same with human beings, as in: "You rescued my soul from the midst of lions' whelps," and what follows. These would come from limbs and senses. 10. The opposition of God's will to evil it names wrath and anger, since among us hostility toward what is opposed to us arises in this way. As in: "From then is your anger," meaning: "From the beginning and always you have by nature been opposed to evil"; and: "Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you." These would come from movements of the soul. 11. His choosing to help his own and to punish his enemies it calls God's rising and awakening. As in: "Arise, O Lord, help us." These would come from movements of the body. 12. It calls God's testing the bringing into action of what is in the minds of his own people, so as to make them more illustrious, more distinguished and more admired. As in: "God tested

[?] it names forgetting. As in: "You forget our poverty." 14. The carrying out of a purpose in deed it calls the full certainty of God's knowledge, since among us deeds are more trustworthy than words. As in: "I will go down, then, and see whether they are doing according to the outcry against them that has come to me; and if not, that I may know"; and: "Now I know that you fear

15. The inescapability of God's justice it calls searching. As in: "And it shall be in that day that I will search Jerusalem with a lamp." These would come from passions of the soul. 16. His postponement of retribution against his enemies (5), and his slowness in helping his own, it calls drowsiness, sleep and heaviness of head. As in: "Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?"; and: "He who keeps Israel will not slumber nor sleep." These would come from passions of the body. 17. A way of life of ours that is pleasing to God it very fittingly names his love. 18. And hatred, walking the opposite way to his

19. And jealousy, his avenging of his own. As in: "The Lord was jealous for his land." These would come from dispositions. 20. The close bond of Jerusalem and of Samaria with God it calls God's betrothal. By metonymy it refers to the inhabitants in feminine terms, after their cities, by a metaphor taken from women. As in: "I will betroth you to myself for

[?] Just so it calls attachment to idols adultery, on account of which Jerusalem also receives a bill of divorce into her hands. 22. No less does it show God's high regard for them by the title of Father, and by that of Firstborn. These would come from common conventions. 23. God's power and judgement it names his sitting (1) and his throne, since among us those who have authority to judge and punish hold their inquiries seated on thrones. As in: "You sat upon a throne, you who judge righteousness"; and: "God sits upon his holy throne"; and: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever"; and: "He who sits upon the cherubim." These would come from ranks. 24. His creative activity it presents sometimes as working by command, as with the rest of creation, and sometimes as his own handiwork, as in our case. And he is said to paint Jerusalem, and to hedge up the way,

and to set a net and a casting-net to catch the wicked. These would come from occupations. 25. His alliance with us for victory and the setting up of trophies it calls nearness, being taken up and exaltation. As in: "The Lord is near to the brokenhearted." 26. Distance, on the other hand, is the delay of that alliance. As in: "Why, O Lord, do you stand far off?" These would come from places. 27. Our experience of the way in which he appears as helper it names his clothing, by analogy with our own usage. As in: "The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with majesty"; and: "Wrapping himself in light as in a garment." These would come from clothing. 28. God's refusal to accept the soul's supplications it fittingly names casting away, because the soul is steeped in evils, and it begs again to be set free. As in: "Why do you cast off my soul?" These would come from customs. 29. The delay of his favour it calls the turning away of hands. As in: "Why do you turn away your hand, even your right hand?" These would come from gestures. 30. It speaks of the soul and flesh of God, however, when it is speaking of him not with regard to relation or activity but more particularly of him himself; just as "Heal my soul" means "Heal me," and "My flesh shall dwell in hope" means "I shall." The firmness and stability of his kingdom it expresses as "prepared." As in: "Your throne is prepared from of old," meaning: "From the beginning it is stable and immovable"; and: "Righteousness and judgement are the preparation of your throne"; and: "In the heavens your truth shall be prepared." And it says that God reigns when, having overcome his enemies, he raises up his own. As in: "The Lord reigns; let the peoples be angry, and [?]." These, then, are the things we have set out, as far as it was right to reason about God, not presuming to think anything beyond them. So much for the idioms of sense. The idioms of wording are as follows. 1. Instead of doing or enjoying a thing, it sometimes says "hear," sometimes "see," and sometimes "know." "Hear," as in: "You will make me hear joy and gladness," instead of "You will give me joy." "See," as in: "To see the goodness of your chosen ones," instead of "To enjoy your goodness that attends us." "Know," as in: "You have made known to me the ways [of life]," instead of "You have made me enjoy life." 2. "Teach" instead of "grant," as in: "And teach me that you are God my Saviour." 3. "He spoke," often of God, instead of "he declared," as in: "God has spoken in his holy place." 4. "Once" for what is unchangeable, as in: "God has spoken once"; and: "Once I have sworn."

5. A responsive exchange on the part of the whole people signifies the common prosperity. As in: "O Lord, save us now; O Lord, prosper us now; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," as though each one of the people were saying it; to which it adds: "We have blessed you from the house of the Lord." 6. It uses "there" not only of place but also of actions. As in: "There is the way by which I will show him my salvation," that is, to the sacrifice, for punishment [?]; and: "There all the workers of iniquity fell." 7. Often it uses "righteousness" when a person speaks of himself without testifying to his own virtue of life, and then likewise when he speaks of others. As in: "Hear, O Lord, my righteousness," and the like, as of one who justly receives help from God, or of God as justly giving it. 8. It often uses "love" of God to express intensity. As in: "The Lord loves mercy and judgement"; and: "For the Lord loves judgement"; and: "He has loved righteousness," instead of "He is eager to judge justly"; and: "For behold, you have loved truth." 9. It often expresses comparisons metaphorically, so as to present an emphasis greater than what is actually said. As in: "To him who rides upon the heaven of heaven toward the east," meaning "from the first and from the beginning," by a metaphor from the fact that the east is where the day begins. And: "From the height of days I shall not fear"; here too "from the height" means "from above and from the beginning." And: "The assembly of bulls," instead of "of very great ones." 10. It uses the word "as" in two ways: either for comparison or for affirmation. For comparison, as in: "Make them like a wheel, like stubble." For affirmation, as in: "How good is God to Israel," instead of saying "Exceedingly good"; and: "We became as those who are comforted"; and: "We beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father," instead of "truly the Only-begotten." 11. It also signifies some of the things it means by what goes along with them. As in: "They will sojourn and hide," meaning "They gather and lie in ambush," since anyone who goes off to another place certainly sojourns there, away from his own people. 12. It uses "hide," when speaking of God, to mean "guard." As in: "You will hide them in the secret place of your presence," instead of "You will guard them"; and: "He hid me in his tent"; and: "How great is the abundance of your goodness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you," meaning "which you keep for those who fear you"; and: "Of your hidden ones," as if to say "of those kept by you." It is used of us too, as in: "In my heart I have hidden your words." 13. Of us it also says "sleep" for "rest." As in: "If you lie down among the

lots"; and: "In peace I will both lie down and sleep." 14. It often uses "bosom" of what is inseparable. As in: "Render to our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom," instead of "Grant them your manifold punishment, never to be parted from them"; and: "[The reproach] of many nations, which I have borne in my bosom"; and: "My prayer shall return into my bosom"; and: "From the midst of your bosom to the end"; and: "The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known." 15. It calls what is unstable a lie, or a liar. As in: "Every man is a liar." 16. It joins truth to God's mercy because of their security and infallibility. As in: "Mercy and truth have met"; and: "Let your mercy and your truth uphold me continually"; and: "You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is all around you"; and: "His mercy and truth, who will [?]?" 17. "To wash the hands" means not to share in some matter, since this was laid down by law for the ancients. As in: "I will wash my hands among the innocent"; and: "He will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner," instead of "He will show himself innocent of that man's punishment." So too Pilate

18. It often speaks of likeness instead of the thing itself. As in: "And I shall be like those who go down into the pit," instead of "I shall go down." 19. It often calls heaven "heavens." As in: "Praise the Lord from the heavens." 20. It often states comparisons without "as." As in: "And he brought me up from a pit of misery"; and: "He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire"; and: "We went through fire and water"; and: "They go up [?]"; and: "Judah is a lion's whelp"; and: "To Adam there came a vision of assault [?]"; and: "The wolf shall feed with the lamb"; and: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse"; and: "Behold, I am preparing your stone as carbuncle"; and: "Stallions mad for mares"; and: "For fire has devoured the beauties of the wilderness"; and: "It is a tree of life"; and: "Thorns grow in the hand of a drunkard"; and: "I was turned to misery while a thorn was fixed in me"; and: "They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ"; and: "Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly." 21. It indicates an action by a limb. For example: "The iniquity of my heel will surround me," instead of "of my action"; and: "They will watch my heel"; and: "He has already supplanted me" (literally, "heeled me"), instead of (5) "He has tripped me up"; hence he was called "Supplanter."

“tongues,” instead of “voices”; and “He added an ear to me,” instead of “obedience”; and “the tongue of your dogs,” instead of “the lapping”; and “He heard a tongue that he did not know.” 22. It often says “the way” instead of “conduct,” as in “Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk”; and “The priests hid the way,” meaning their own conduct; and “Set your hearts on your ways”; and “Why have you made us stray from your way?”; and “Your ways and your doings have done these things to you”; and “so that if he found any who were of the Way”; and “I persecuted this Way”; and “According to the Way which they call a sect, so I worship.” 23. It often says “endurance” instead of “expectation,” or “to endure” instead of “to expect,” as in “And now what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?”, meaning “my expectation and hope”; and the passage in Jeremiah, “Endurance of Israel, O Lord”; and “I endured, waiting for someone to grieve with me”; and “Endure for the Lord”; and “Endure for me, says the Lord”; and “while they endured

24. It often speaks of things that are not causes as though they were causes, as in “So that your foot may be dipped in blood,” instead of “by every necessity” [?]; and “Against you alone have I sinned, [?]”; “So that I may show my power in you”; and “So that the righteousness of the Lord may be known”; and “I came into the world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see”; and “The law came in so that the trespass might increase”; and “so that every mouth may be stopped”; and “so that you may not do the things you want.” 25. It indicates an action by association, as in “And I will not go in with lawbreakers,” instead of “I will not break the law”; and “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” instead of “who has not acted ungodly”; and “I did not sit in the council of those who make merry”; and “Let my soul not enter into their counsel.” 26. It uses the oath of what is certain, as in “I have sworn to David my servant”; and “The Lord swore truth to David”; and “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord”; and “The Lord swears by the pride of Jacob.” 27. It often shows a disposition through words, as in “They said, ‘Who will see them?’”, instead of “They did everything as though there were no one watching over them”; and “For he said in his heart, ‘There is no God’”; and “They said, ‘Come, let us wipe them out as a nation’”; and “Let us take possession of God’s sanctuary for ourselves”; and “Their kindred together said in their hearts.”

28. Evil, that is, wickedness, it often uses for punishment, as in “He sent out against them the wrath of his anger [?]”; and “I who make peace and create evils,” meaning that he allows peace and permits war; and “Add evils to them, O Lord”; and “Evils came down from the Lord”; and “Sarah did evil to Hagar her maidservant”; and “They will do evil to it,” instead of “they will make it suffer”; and “They have done evil to your inheritance”; and “repenting of the evils,” instead of “of the punishments for offences”; and “There is no evil in cities”; and “Sufficient for the day is its own evil,” instead of saying that the work done in it brings people countless toils and labours. 29. It often takes “cup” for punishment, as in “Fire and brimstone and a stormy wind shall be the portion of their cup”; and “Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling”; and “You shall drink your sister’s cup”; and the Lord: “The cup that I am about to drink.” 30. It uses “the name” of the Lord instead of his having it as his own, as in “Let them know that your name is Lord,” meaning “You are the Lord”; and “Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time,” instead of [?]

31. It figures God’s punishments metaphorically as fire, sword and arrows, as in “Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one.” 32. It uses the number seven for abundance, or as a perfect number, as in “Seven times a day,” instead of “often”; and “Repay our neighbours sevenfold”; and “She set up seven pillars.” 33. It often speaks about God as though making a change of person, as in “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God”; and “Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one — peoples will fall beneath you — in the heart of the king’s enemies,” that is, of your mighty king; and “In the image of God he made man”; and “God rained fire and brimstone on Sodom from the Lord”; and “May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord”; and “who was declared Son of God by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

34. It often takes “morning” for speed, as in “God will help her very early in the morning”; and “Morning by morning he will give his judgment,” that is, immediately; and “like the dawn,” that is, suddenly. 35. It often calls joy, or life, light, and grief, or death, darkness, because those who live in good cheer are somehow more far-sighted in their affairs, while those sunk in despondency cannot even see what lies at their feet; and because seeing the light belongs to the living, while the dying remain in darkness. Joy or life, then, it calls light, as in “Light has dawned for the righteous”; and “My God, you will light up my darkness,” instead of “You will turn my grief into joy”; and “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun”; and “Shine, shine, Jerusalem”; and “If I walk in darkness, the Lord will be my light,” that is, on the contrary, while I was expecting misfortune and affliction, some joy and festivity met me unexpectedly. Grief and death it calls darkness, as in “And I said, ‘Surely darkness will trample me’”; and “Night is illumination in my delight”; and “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me”; and “They laid me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death.” 36. It speaks of the dissolution of the elements in the case of things that are darkened and cannot be seen, as in “The sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will not give their light”; and “The Lord will utter his voice before his host, for his camp is exceedingly great.” 37. God’s permitting of human evils it speaks of as his own action, since, though able to prevent it, he does not do so, as in “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness”; and “Do not turn away in anger from your servant”; and “You turned our paths aside from your way”; and “Behold, I lead her astray,” about Jerusalem; and “Why, O Lord, have you made us stray from your way? Why have you hardened our hearts so that we do not fear you?”; and “I will surely harden the heart of Pharaoh and of his servants”; and “God gave them over to a debased mind.” 38. It often expresses God’s power through action, as in “He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble”; and “He who rebukes the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers desolate”; and “[At his feet] he stood, and the earth was shaken; he looked, and the nations melted.” 39. It often speaks of “the flesh,” either of the flesh itself, as in “They gave the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth,” or of baseness, as in “My spirit shall not remain in men [?]” [?]. Note (6): “will not give”: [?]; the printed editions have “will not set.”

40. It says “son” instead of “man”: “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man?”, instead of “man”; and “Son of man,” instead of “Man”; and “a lion’s whelp,” instead of “a lion”; and “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter,” and “like a lamb, silent before its shearer.” 41. It uses the name “spirit” in many ways: for will, for a gift, for an angel, for the soul, for the voice, or for the air. For the will of God, as in “You made covenants, but not by my spirit,” instead of “will”; and “He will change his spirit,” instead of “will.” For our will, as in “And renew a right spirit within me,” that is, will; and “Its spirit was not faithful to God,” that is, its will; and “They went astray by a spirit of fornication”; and “Ephraim, an evil spirit”; and “because another spirit was found in him”; and “Now, bound in the spirit, I am going to Jerusalem”; and the Lord: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” For a gift, as in “And uphold me with a guiding spirit”; and “A spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and might, a spirit of knowledge and godliness, a spirit of the fear of God will fill him”; and “Let a double portion of your spirit come upon me”; and the Apostle often calls the gift “spirit,” for example, “Do not quench the Spirit.” For an angel, as in “And a spirit came upon me, and took me up and lifted me.” For the soul, as in “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth.” For the voice, as in “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host”; and the Apostle: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also.” For the air, as in “With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish”; and “You sent your wind; the sea covered them”; and “Let it come from the four winds.”

42. It often uses “until” not of time but of the matter itself, as in “And in the shadow of your wings I will hope until lawlessness passes away” — for he was not going to give up his hope in God after that; and “until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”; and “I am he, until you grow old”; and “Seek the Lord until the fruits of righteousness come to you”; and “Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death”; and “Behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age”; and “He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son.” 43. It constantly uses an exchange of tenses: the future instead of the past, as in “Every night I will wash my bed,” instead of “I washed” [?]; and “They will pass through the river on foot,” instead of “they passed through”; and “Like a swallow, so I will cry.” And the past instead of the future, as in “I cried to God, and the Lord heard me,” instead of “will hear me”; and “Then the princes of Edom hastened.” And the future instead of the present, as in “They will dwell as strangers and will hide,” instead of “they dwell as strangers”; and “They will utter and will speak.” 44. It speaks of “the age” in three ways: either as the lifetime of each person, or as the whole extent of time, or as what is perpetual and endless. Of the lifetime of each person, as in “And he laboured for the age, and will live to the end”; and “You gave him length of days for an age of ages”; and “For ever I will confess you” — as long as I live and exist; and “He who dwells in Jerusalem will not be shaken for ever”; and “He will serve you for ever”; and “You shall not wash my feet for ever”; and “I will not eat meat for ever”; and “He will not thirst for

Of the whole extent of time, as in “He will go to the generation of his fathers; until the age he will not see light,” instead of “as long as the present state of things remains,” for he did not speak without limit so as to do away with the resurrection; and “He gave them an everlasting reproach,” of the foreigners, meaning a long-lasting one, so that they would be remembered as most shameful even by later generations; and “The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance”; and “Israel is saved by the Lord with an everlasting salvation”; and “Nor shall they be put to shame until the age on Mount Zion, from now and for ever,” instead of “for a long time.” And “Judea will be inhabited for ever.” Note (7): “Until” often: “until” is by no means set in opposition to the future; it states what holds up to this point, but does not deny what comes after. Note (8): [?] “be put to shame.” Another reading: “and they will not be put to shame.”

Of what is perpetual and endless, as in “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever”; and “For ever, O Lord, your word abides in heaven”; and “The Lord abides for ever, and his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom”; and the Lord says, “He will receive a hundredfold in this present age, and in the age to come he will inherit eternal life”; and “And this is eternal life”; and “I will give them eternal life.” It expresses wishes in the form of commands, as in “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living,” instead of “may they be blotted out and not be written”; and “By the greatness of your arm let them be turned to stone,” instead of “may they be turned to stone”; and “May my life go up from corruption.” Beginning of the matters concerning composition. These would be peculiar [?] to blessed David. By ellipsis, as in “But like chaff, which the wind drives away from the face of the earth” — “will be” is missing; and also “having said” or “saying,” or “you said,” or “they say,” or something of the kind. “Having said,” as in “To the Lord in my affliction I cried,” having said, “What profit is there in my blood?” — the tense has been exchanged; and “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord,” having said, “O Lord, deliver my soul.” “Saying,” as in “I will sing and make music to the Lord,” saying — for there is no change of person in the psalms. “You said,” as in “When I seize the appointed time, I will judge uprightly”; and “I will give you understanding and instruct you.” For “saying” in the plural, as in “Against the Lord and against his Christ,” saying. For “they say,” as in “And do not speak unrighteousness against God,” instead of “they say”; “Not at all from the desert mountains.” It uses tautology everywhere, as in “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me”; and “I lay down and slept”; and “Both the earthborn and the sons of men”; and “He who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire”; and “The Lord became my refuge, and my God the helper of my hope”; and “The Lord spoke and called [?] the earth”; and “They will utter and will speak”; and “Give ear to my words, O Lord.” [?] It often says the same thing by a kind of inversion, as in “you see,” instead of “because you see” [?]; and “Yours is the arm,” instead of “Your arm.” And it makes the inversion over a longer stretch, as in “Among your remnants you will prepare their face,” instead of “among their remnants”; as such things are also found among the lyric poets [?].

“the poor man, because the sinner is praised” — these are taken together with something set in between; and “For day and night your hand was heavy upon me, while a thorn was fixed in me” — for “I was turned to misery, through my crying all day long” is fittingly assigned to it; and “Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one,” with “peoples” set in between. It says the same thing by way of intensification, as in “Chastening, the Lord has chastened me”; and “Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” And “Surely, blessing, I will bless you.” It often uses “behold” superfluously, as in “For behold, you have loved truth”; “Behold, the virgin shall conceive.” And “nevertheless,” which contributes nothing at all, as in “Nevertheless, he is disquieted in vain.” And “with,” as in “The Lord tests with the righteous and with the ungodly”; and “God will judge with the righteous and with the ungodly.” And “for,” as in “The clouds gave forth a voice, for indeed your arrows go abroad”; and “For indeed those who refuse to dwell”; and “For you are my brother.” And indeed also the particle “ge,” which one can find not rarely in most of them, but especially in the book of Kingdoms and in Solomon. Blessed David, however, uses “in” instead of “with,” as in “and mountains be moved in the hearts of the seas”; and “in burnt offerings,” instead of “with burnt offerings”; and “in peace together”; and “But I walked in my innocence”; and “God has gone up in a shout”; and “The voice of the Lord in strength, the voice of the Lord in majesty.” The diligent, then, borrowing their starting points from here, will find a road and a gate for their love of learning, to be guided toward the meaning of holy Scripture. Its most general modes are also these: by metaphor, by parable, by comparison, by synecdoche, by example, by metonymy, by antiphrasis, by periphrasis, by recapitulation or resumption, by catachresis, by personification, by figuration, by allegory, by hyperbole, by mockery, by irony, by sarcasm, by riddle, by threat, by denial, by aposiopesis, by exhortation — besides, of course, the idioms.

By metaphor, when it transfers to some things what belongs to others, whether by action or by nature — for instance, to us and to God — as in “The Lord shepherds me”; and “to shepherd Jacob his servant”; and “Should the shepherds feed themselves?”; and “My sheep were scattered, because there were no shepherds”; and “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” For it often calls the seizures of God’s justice nets and casting-nets, for example, “I will spread my net over him”; and the devastation wrought by enemies a flood

By metonymy, when it renames either the things contained after their containers, or the places inhabited after their inhabitants. The things contained after their containers, as in “And your cup inebriating me, as the very best”; and “Wail, ships of Carthage”; and “You shall drink your sister’s cup.” The places inhabited after their inhabitants, as in “He will summon the heaven above”; and “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets”; and “Rejoice, you many islands.” By antiphrasis, when it shows one thing by its opposite, for example, “Surely he will bless you to your face,” instead of “curse”; and “He blessed God and the king,” instead of “he insulted, he wronged”; and “How the king has been glorified!”; and “Let that man be merry.” By periphrasis, when it wraps a longer phrasing around what could be expressed in a few words, for example, “And behold, the foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians — these were born there.” By recapitulation or resumption, when things introduced at length and in various ways are, because of the difficulty arising from the irregularity of the digressions, gone over again in
a few words, as Moses says, “This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth.” There are such things also in Kingdoms, and in the [?]

By catachresis, when it misapplies the name of some things to others as well, for example, “Guard me, O Lord, as the apple of the eye”; and “In you we will butt down our enemies with the horn”; and “He who roofs his upper chambers with waters”; and “Like the dawn a great and mighty people will be spread over the mountains,” speaking of the locust. By personification, when it assigns persons and speech to things that are inanimate, and sometimes even to things that have no substance. To inanimate things, as in “Be lifted up, you everlasting gates”; and “The heavens declare”; and “The trees went forth.” To things without substance, as in “Righteousness and peace have kissed”; and “The Lord called for judgment by fire”; and “He threw the stone into the mouth of lawlessness”; and “Wisdom said, ‘The Lord created me’”; and “I was the one in whom he delighted daily”; and “She built herself a house.” By figuration, when it gives shape to things for the exposition of events, as in “The queen stood at your right hand”; and “The rivers will clap their hands together”; and “Your breasts were raised and your hair sprang up, but you were naked and shameful” — calling the mountains breasts by catachresis, from their shape, and calling the earth’s fruitfulness hair. It also constructs figuration out of events, as in the story of blessed Job, for example, “The devil stood before God.” By allegory, when it constantly calls countless multitudes waters, and their onslaught a flood; and “He will be like the tree planted”; and the Apostle allegorizes Hagar. By hyperbole, when in many cases it uses a greater magnitude of expression than what happens, or exists, or is possible, as in “They go up to the heavens,” of seafarers; and “But God will crush the heads of his enemies”; and “Every night I will wash my bed”; and “The mountains skipped like rams”; and “The trees of the field will clap their branches”; and “It is easier for a camel”; and of the locust, “For a nation has come up against my land, mighty; its teeth are a lion’s teeth”; and “The sinners have been estranged from the womb”; and “Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing”; and “If your right eye makes you stumble, pluck it out”; and “If you are silent, the stones will cry

[?] …will [?]; and, "One iota or one stroke"; and, "The heavens and the earth will pass away." By way of taunting, when he speaks over the shame of enemies: "Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it"; and, "Take a harp, roam about, play the harp well"; "For ships no longer come from Carthage"; "A fair and charming city, mistress of sorceries"; "She did not trust in the Lord"; and, "Prophesy to us, Christ, who is it that [?]" By irony, when he mocks worthlessness by means of praise: as, "Gather to him his holy ones"; and, "Jerusalem, a vine with fine branches"; and, "Where is the dwelling place of the lions, and the lion's whelp?"; and, "Asps and the offspring of asps ran to the Egyptians"; and, "Hades below was embittered when it met you"; and, "You have been taken, just as [?]"; and, "Your glory has gone down to Hades [?] … beneath you they will spread decay." By sarcasm, when he means to praise by way of extreme lowliness: as, "I am a worm and not a man"; and, "After whom are you chasing, O king? After a single leaf, and after a dead dog"; and other such passages. By riddle, when the account is set forth obscurely [?]: for example, "Your silver is counterfeit; your wine-sellers mix the wine with water"; and, "Say to every bird and to all the beasts"; and, "Send out the sickles, for the harvest has come"; and, "See, the axe is laid at the root of the trees."

By threat, when he threatens through God: "If you do not turn back, he will polish his sword"; and, "Bear fruit worthy of repentance"; and, "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." By declaration, when he defines the bringing of good things and of evil things as settled and complete, both the captivity and the return. By reticence, when he shows a renewal from God: as, "And Jerusalem shall be holy, and foreigners shall no longer pass through her" — [?] the qualification "unless perhaps they transgress" he passed over in silence; and, "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit" — the birth through blood he held in reserve. By exhortation, when everything in the divinely inspired Scripture together, whether through words or through deeds, rightly seems to contribute to this end. There are, however, two kinds of divine Scripture, the prophetic

and the historical. Yet each of them is made up of three times: past, present and future. Past, as Moses' account of the constitution of the universe; present, as the words of the most blessed Elisha to Gehazi about the gold that had been given him; future, as the prophets' sayings concerning the Hebrews and the coming of Christ, which we have received through words, visions and deeds. Through words, as, "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah"; through visions, as, "And the hand of the Lord came upon me"; and, "The dead will rise"; and, "I watched until thrones were set in place"; and, "Behold, with the clouds one like a son of man coming"; through deeds, as in the case of Abraham: "Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove and a pigeon," and what follows; and, "Take your beloved son, whom you love, Isaac." This being so, those who are learning ought first of all to fix their minds on the subject matter of the sayings, and only then apply to them, as is fitting, the word-by-word interpretation; for if the sense is not established beforehand, the construction of the words will go astray. Just as with those who steer ships: unless some definite place is set before them as a goal, toward which they will direct every movement of the tillers, they are forced to entrust their craft now to this wind, now to that, and are carried all over the sea, fleeing into aimless wandering as if into a harbor. So it will necessarily happen also in expounding doctrine, whenever it is put forward without some underlying subject. For how would it not be the height of absurdity if the learned cannot introduce even the rhapsodies, which are made up of fictions and not true events, in any other way than by first bringing the subject of each to their hearers' knowledge, so that they may rightly direct their use of words toward it and not to the winds; while we subject the contents of our divine record [?] to mere conjectures, not ashamed to impose on them random and incoherent [?] interpretations? Therefore, just as for those setting out for a completely unknown country, those who have experience of it ought before all else to point out the path leading there, by which they are to travel, and then also make known to them the signs along [?] the way, by following which they would in no way stray from the straight road, so one might lay down the same rule for those who profess to teach. First, they must make the subject of the matters known to their pupils, toward which these must necessarily direct the inclination of their own minds; then the knowledge of the idioms of Scripture, the recognition of its figures and the discernment of its tropes; and not least the [?] of word-by-word interpretation, showing it in advance like some [?] of the journey, through

which the goal set before them may be safe and secure [?]. For it is clear that, for those who mean to fly rather than to walk along a road, the [?] of signs is superfluous and useless. Above all, one must hold firmly and resolutely to the sequence of the whole; whoever holds on to it carefully, like a thread stretched out along the design [?], toward reaching the precise sense, will not miss what is fitting. Indeed, the sense of the words is to be put in the place of a body, and the contemplation in the place of the shape that belongs to the body. For the one can be shown all at once even from a distance, while the other is presented more precisely through the limbs and their arrangement, without imagining anything beyond the body. Let this too be known to our own people: of prophecy, some has been spoken in prose, like that of Isaiah and Jeremiah and anyone else of their kind; and some in meter with song, like the Psalms of the blessed David and the songs of Moses in Exodus and Deuteronomy. But whatever was spoken in meter, though not with song, and handed down from of old, could never be prophecy; and such are the rest of the books written in verse, like Job and the books of Solomon. The end, with God.
